To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative risk (odds ratio) of schizophrenia in Rhesus D maternal–fetal incompatibility-incompatible children is increased, and that this risk increases with the number previous incompatible pregnancies in the family.

(i) there is evidence that schizophrenia is more common in RHD MFI-incompatible children, and that (ii) this effect is consistent with the hypothesis that the risk of schizophrenia is increased in RHD MGI-incompatible children who have experienced Rh incompatibility diseases in previous pregnancies.
the relative risk for RHD MFG schizophrenia increases with birth order and the relative risk for schizophrenia in RHD incompatible second-born and later-born children is 1·7.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possible effects of Rh incompatibilities between the mother and the fetus, which may be a factor in schizophrenia.

the hypothesis that schizophrenia is a consequence of Rh incompatiblity disease, which in turn is caused by a combination of maternal–fetal Rh genotype incompatibility, and maternal immune system overreaction to Rh-positive fetal blood.
the hypothesis that maternal-fetal genotype incompatibilities (MFGs) may be risk factors for schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence is consistent with an association between Rh incompatibility and an increased risk of developing schizophrenia, but the evidence is still not strong enough to rule out the possibility that this is a chance finding.
there is significant evidence that the maternal genotype and MFG incompatibilities increase the risk of RHD and Rh incompatibility diseases and, consequently, schizophrenia.
RHD MFG incompatible children have an increased risk of being diagnosed with schizophrenia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of schizophrenia in an RHD MFG–incompatible child is 1.6 times greater than that in an RHD-compatible child.
the MFG-incompatibility test provides a useful tool for identifying genetic risk factors that interact with maternal genotype.
the evidence that maternal-fetal genotype incompatibilities contribute to the risk of schizophrenia has increased.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MFG test can be extended to include any number and any order of siblings.

the MFG test can be applied to case–parent trio studies that have multiple siblings, and the results can be used to estimate the effect of previous RHD-incompatible pregnancies on RHD MFG risk in the later-born children.
the MFG test is a powerful and flexible method for detecting maternal-genotype and maternal-fetal genotype interactions in the etiology of schizophrenia and other disorders.
